sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Compute answers where the work actually runs. The exam asks you to match virtual servers, instance families, containers, serverless compute, scaling, and traffic distribution to the right requirement.
sections.callout: Match the compute requirement to the right AWS service.

sections.title: Amazon EC2
paragraphs: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) provides resizable virtual compute capacity. The customer has significant control over the operating system and software running on an instance.
sections.callout: Virtual server or OS-level control → Amazon EC2

sections.title: EC2 Instance Types
paragraphs: Different workloads need different combinations of CPU, memory, storage, and networking. EC2 instance families provide resource profiles suited to those workload needs.

entries.title: General Purpose
paragraphs: Balances compute, memory, and networking for workloads without one dominant resource need.

entries.title: Compute Optimized
paragraphs: Provides a high ratio of compute power for processor-intensive workloads.

entries.title: Memory Optimized
paragraphs: Supports workloads requiring large amounts of RAM or in-memory processing.

entries.title: Storage Optimized
paragraphs: Supports workloads requiring high local-storage throughput or high random I/O.

sections.title: Containers
paragraphs: Containers package application code and dependencies into portable units that run consistently across compatible environments.

entries.title: Amazon ECS
paragraphs: Amazon Elastic Container Service is AWS-native managed container orchestration.

entries.title: Amazon EKS
paragraphs: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service provides a managed Kubernetes control plane.

sections.title: Serverless Compute
paragraphs: Serverless means AWS manages the underlying infrastructure while the customer focuses on application code or container workloads. It does not mean that servers do not exist.

entries.title: AWS Lambda
paragraphs: Runs event-driven functions without requiring the customer to provision or manage servers.

entries.title: AWS Fargate
paragraphs: Provides serverless compute capacity for supported container workloads.

table.caption: Choose the serverless model that matches the workload
rows: Run containers without managing underlying servers

sections.title: Auto Scaling
paragraphs: Auto scaling adjusts capacity as demand changes. Resources can grow when demand rises and contract when demand falls, supporting elasticity instead of permanently provisioning for peak load.
sections.callout: Automatically adjust capacity to demand → Auto Scaling

sections.title: Load Balancers
paragraphs: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across healthy targets. This helps avoid overloading one resource and supports application availability, scalability, and performance.
sections.callout: Distribute incoming application traffic → Load balancer

table.caption: These capabilities often cooperate but solve different problems
rows: How many resources do I need?

sections.title: GSA Scenario Recognition
bullets: Virtual server with OS control → EC2
Incoming requests are distributed → Load balancer

entries.title: ECS vs. EKS
paragraphs: AWS-native container orchestration → ECS. Kubernetes → EKS.

entries.title: Lambda vs. Fargate
paragraphs: Run functions or event-driven code → Lambda. Run containers without server management → Fargate.

entries.title: Auto Scaling vs. Load Balancing
paragraphs: Auto Scaling changes capacity. A load balancer distributes traffic.

entries.title: Compute vs. Memory vs. Storage
paragraphs: CPU clue → Compute optimized. RAM clue → Memory optimized. Local disk and I/O clue → Storage optimized.

entries.title: Serverless Trap
paragraphs: Serverless means AWS manages the underlying servers; it does not mean no servers exist.
